UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Case No. 1:26-cv-02331
V.
KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED
CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC.;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,
Defendants.
MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF'S RENEWED RULE 56 MOTION FOR
PARTIAL SUMMARY JUDGMENT
I.
NCMEC AND HALL DESCRIBE THE APRIL 22, 2026 LETTERS AS HALL'S
WORK FOR NCMEC
NCMEC has told this Court how the two April 22, 2026 letters came to be. "On April 22,
2026, NCMEC responded to the subpoenas without awaiting formal service via two substantively-
identical letters signed by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC." ECF
No. 11 at 2. Hall "adopts and joins in" that memorandum. ECF No. 45 at 1. The letters bear
NCMEC's letterhead. Each carries Hall's signature above the title "Corporate Counsel." ECF No.
7-5 at 2-3. In the earlier action over the same letters, NCMEC and Hall, through the counsel who
represents both of them here, told this Court that Hall "was clearly acting in the course and scope
of her employment in responding to the subpoenas." ECF No. 7-4 at 7.
1

Plaintiff renews the request the Court denied on August 12, 2026, "without prejudice to
renewal at an appropriate time." ECF No. 12 at 1. The request is narrow. Plaintiff asks the Court
to determine under Rule 56(a) that Hall acted as NCMEC's employee and agent, within the course
and scope of her employment, when she signed and issued the two letters on NCMEC's behalf.
That determination resolves the agency-and-scope component of NCMEC's potential vicarious
liability under Counts I, II, III, and VI. ECF No. 5 9 21. It resolves nothing else.
If the Court does not grant that relief in full, Plaintiff asks the Court to consider, under Rule
56(g), the same determination and seventeen numbered facts. The facts concern Hall's
employment, the April 9, 2026 transmission, the absence of formal service, the wording of the
letters, what the letters omit, and the names under which Plaintiff operated Meta accounts. Each
rests on a document in the record, a statement of NCMEC or Hall, or Plaintiff's sworn testimony
about his own conduct.
The Motion does not ask what any CyberTipline report contains. It does not ask whether
the letters were true, whether any privilege or immunity applies, whether Defendants agreed with
one another, or what anyone intended. The submitted issue is the capacity in which Hall acted.
The evidence on that issue comes from NCMEC and Hall.
II. THE RESPONSE POSTURE AND THE EVIDENTIARY RECORD HAVE
CHANGED SINCE AUGUST 12, 2026
A.
The August 12 Order.
The Court denied the original motion "without prejudice to renewal at an appropriate time."
ECF No. 12 at 1. The Order identified two circumstances. Plaintiff had filed the First Amended
Complaint and the motion on the same day. And "Defendants' answers or other responses to the
Original Complaint are not due until August 21, 2026." Id. The Order found the motion premature
on that basis.
2

ECF No. 11 was docketed on August 12, 2026, before ECF No. 12. ECF No. 12 denied the
original motion because responses were not yet due; it did not address the merits. Hall's adoption
of ECF No. 11 (ECF No. 45, Sept. 2, 2026) and Plaintiff's two declarations (ECF Nos. 31, 59-2)
came after ECF No. 12
The change since August 12 is not the passage of time. The response posture the Order
identified has changed: each appearing Defendant has responded. And the record has expanded.
NCMEC's memorandum states the capacity in which Hall acted and states that NCMEC issued
the letters before formal service. ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. Hall adopted those statements. ECF No.
3

45 at 1. Plaintiff's declarations supply testimony, on personal knowledge, about the names he used
on Meta's services and the reason his legal name appears in the April 9 materials. ECF No. 31 99
2-7; ECF No. 59-2 19 2-10. The letters, the April 9 materials, and the earlier joint filing of
NCMEC and Hall were before the Court in August and remain in the record. ECF Nos. 7-4, 7-5,
7-6.
C. Local Civil Rule 56.
Rule 56(b) permits a motion for summary judgment "at any time until 30 days after the
close of all discovery" unless "a different time is set by local rule or the court orders otherwise."
Local Civil Rule 56(A) sets a different time for this District and displaces that default. "The time
provisions of Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(b) shall not apply in this District." The Court's Order supplies the
operative instruction here: renewal "at an appropriate time." ECF No. 12 at 1. Local Civil Rule
56(C) requires leave of Court for separate motions for summary judgment on separate grounds.
This Motion renews the one ground presented in ECF No. 6. Its alternative request under Rule
56(g) concerns the same submission and is not a separate ground.
The timing argument is this. The Court reserved renewal. The parties whose relationship
is at issue have since responded and have described that relationship to the Court. The record now
includes those descriptions and Plaintiff's testimony. That is the record on which the submitted
component can be assessed. The pending Rule 12 motions test the sufficiency of the pleading; this
Motion asks the Court to determine one component on the record.
D.
The Motion rests on the operative pleading and seeks no change to any
discovery or scheduling disposition.
ECF No. 5 is the operative pleading. The Motion rests on it. The declaration at ECF No.
59-2 was filed as an exhibit to a motion for leave to amend, ECF No. 59, which the Court denied.
ECF No. 84. The Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine filed with this Motion ("Ballentine Decl.")
4

restates that testimony. The Motion requests no discovery. It seeks adjudication on existing
evidence, and it asks the Court to modify no order concerning scheduling or discovery.
ECF No. 108 states that "the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain
from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss." ECF No. 108
at 2. This Motion is consistent with ECF Nos. 84 and 108. It seeks no discovery. It rests on
documents already docketed, on testimony Plaintiff has already sworn, and on statements NCMEC
and Hall made in their own filings. It asks the Court to modify neither order. The Fourth Circuit
has identified the risk of early summary judgment where the facts are "exclusively in the control
of the opposing party." Harrods Ltd. v. Sixty Internet Domain Names, 302 F.3d 214, 247 (4th Cir.
2002) (quotation marks and citation omitted); see Part VIII. The facts on the submitted component
are in the control of NCMEC and Hall, and NCMEC and Hall have stated them. A party that has
stated a fact in its own brief does not need discovery to learn it.
The denial of ECF No. 59 is the subject of Plaintiff's pending objections (ECF Nos. 90,
91, 102). Plaintiff also files concurrently a renewed motion for leave to file a Second Amended
Complaint. The proposed pleading retains the claims against Hall and NCMEC to which the
Motion's agency-and-scope request relates. Should leave be granted before determination of the
Motion, Plaintiff requests consideration of the corresponding issue under the resulting operative
pleading, following any supplemental briefing the Court deems necessary, rather than denial solely
because the First Amended Complaint has been superseded.
II.
STATEMENT OF UNDISPUTED MATERIAL FACTS
Under Local Civil Rule 56(B), Plaintiff lists, in numbered paragraphs, the material facts as
to which he contends there is no genuine issue, with citations to the parts of the record relied on.
Each paragraph states a proposition Plaintiff asks the Court to establish. None asserts that the
proposition has already been conclusively admitted. Citations to attachments use the page
5

numbering of the filed ECF document, including exhibit cover pages. ECF Nos. 7-4, 7-5, and 7-6
are re-filed with this Motion as Exhibits 3, 4, and 5 to the accompanying Declaration, and page
citations to them are unchanged. Citations to declarations are to numbered paragraphs.
A.
1.
Hall's employment and the issuance of the letters
Katie Hall was an employee of NCMEC and served as NCMEC's Corporate
Counsel when she signed and issued the two letters dated April 22, 2026 that appear at ECF No.
7-5 at 2-3. ECF No. 7-4 at 3, 7; ECF No. 11 at 2 (letters issued "[o]n April 22, 2026," and "signed
by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC"); ECF No. 11 at 5 n.2; ECF
No. 11 at 8 ("NCMEC or its employee, Defendant Hall"); ECF No. 45 at 1.
Hall signed each of the two letters. Each letter is on NCMEC letterhead. The
signature block of each letter identifies Hall as "Corporate Counsel." ECF No. 7-5 at 2-3; ECF
No. 7-1 9 5 (authenticating the letters as copies reproduced from the exhibits NCMEC and Hall
filed in the earlier action).
The first sentence of the body of each letter states: "In response to your subpoena
issued April 9, 2026, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children ("NCME") provides
its written responses as detailed below." The reference line of one letter identifies the matter as
"Marvelle Ballentine v. Meta Platforms, Inc., et al." The reference line of the other identifies the
matter as "Marvelle Ballentine v. Devin S. Anderson, et al." ECF No. 7-5 at 2-3; see ECF No. 11
at 2-3 (quoting the first sentence).
B.
4.
The April 9, 2026 materials and formal service
On April 9, 2026, Plaintiff transmitted to NCMEC's Legal Department a letter
giving advance notice of intended subpoenas in two separate matters, together with two signed
subpoena forms and a Schedule A for each. The letter stated that each notice was accompanied by
a signed copy of the draft subpoena "that will be formally served after the notice period has run."
6

NCMEC received the materials. ECF No. 7-1 9 6; Ballentine Decl. 19 4-5; ECF No. 7-6 at 2-3
(letter), 4, 7 (subpoena forms), 5, 8 (Schedule A); ECF No. 7-4 at 3 (describing Hall's letters as
written "shortly after receiving the letters"); ECF No. 11 at 2.
5.
No subpoena had been formally served on NCMEC when NCMEC issued the
April 22, 2026 letters. ECF No. 11 at 2 ("NCMEC responded to the subpoenas without awaiting
formal service"); ECF No. 45 at 1 (adopting ECF No. 11); ECF No. 7-4 at 2 ("two subpoenas sent,
but not formally served"); ECF No. 7-4 at 5 ("NCMEC responding without waiting to be formally
served").
Schedule A to each subpoena form directed production of a document sufficient
to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report, referral, or submission
concerning three identifiers. Schedule A listed the identifiers as "(1) Marvelle J. Ballentine," "(2)
Jay Ballentine," and "(3) the account-level identifier jaychizza@icloud.com," and joined them
with "and/or." ECF No. 7-6 at 5, 8; see ECF No. 11 at 2 (quoting Schedule A).
Each April 22, 2026 letter states that NCMEC has received two CyberTipline
reports "concerning (1) Marvelle J. Ballentine, (2) Jay Ballentine, and/or (3) the account-level
identifierjaychizza@icloud.com." The three identifiers and the connector "and/or" in that sentence
are the identifiers and connector that appear in Schedule A. ECF No. 7-5 at 2-3; compare ECF No.
7-6 at 5, 8; see ECF No. 11 at 2-3 (quoting the letters and describing them as "mirroring the
language utilized by Plaintiff in the Schedules").
C.
Plaintiff's account-name history
Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff did not use the name "Marvelle J. Ballentine" to
create, register, identify, maintain, access, or operate any account on any product or service owned
or operated by Meta Platforms, Inc. that Plaintiff used. ECF No. 31 9| 3; ECF No. 59-2 9 6;
Ballentine Decl. 9 6.
7

9.
Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff did not use "Marvelle J. Ballentine" as a
username, profile name, display name, account name, or other identity by which he identified
himself on Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp, Oculus, Meta Quest, or any other Meta
product or service that he used. ECF No. 31 9 4; ECF No. 59-2 9 7; Ballentine Decl. 1 7.
10.
Before April 22, 2026, Plaintiff did not provide "Marvelle J. Ballentine" to Meta
Platforms, Inc. as the name identifying him for purposes of any Meta account that he created,
maintained, or operated, or as the name identifying any such account. This fact concerns the
identification of accounts. It does not concern litigation filings or other communications. ECF No.
3195; ECF No. 59-2 4 8; Ballentine Decl. 4 8.
11.
Plaintiff operated the Facebook account that was the subject of Meta Platforms,
Inc.'s July 4, 2022 enforcement action under the name "Jay Ballentine." ECF No. 59-2 19 3-5;
Ballentine Decl. 19| 9-11; see also ECF No. 31 9 6; ECF No. 59-2 9| 9; Ballentine Decl. 1 12.
12.
Plaintiff included "Marvelle J. Ballentine" in the April 9, 2026 correspondence
and subpoena materials that he transmitted to NCMEC because it is his legal name and the name
under which the underlying federal litigation was pending. He did not include that name because
he had used it to identify or operate any Meta account. ECF No. 31 192, 7; ECF No. 59-2 19 2,
10; Ballentine Decl. 9l 13-14.
D.
13.
What the letters do not identify
Neither letter identifies the electronic service provider or other source that
submitted either report. ECF No. 7-5 at 2-3.
14.
Neither letter supplies a report number for either report. Id.
15.
Neither letter supplies a report-specific date for either report. Each letter refers
only to a period "between July 1, 2022 and the present." Id.
16.
Neither letter states which of the three listed identifiers matched either report. Id.
8

17.
Neither letter identifies any particular Facebook account as the subject of either
report. Id.
IV.
THE GOVERNING STANDARD REQUIRES PLAINTIFF TO ESTABLISH THE
SUBMITTED COMPONENT ON THE RECORD
A.
Rule 56(a) and the burden of a plaintiff-movant.
A party may move for summary judgment on "each claim or defense — or the part of each
claim or defense — on which summary judgment is sought." Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). The Court
"shall grant summary judgment if the movant shows that there is no genuine dispute as to any
material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." Id. A fact is material if it
"might affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law." Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.,
477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986). A dispute is genuine if "the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could
return a verdict for the nonmoving party." Id. The question is whether the evidence presents a
sufficient disagreement to require submission to a jury or is so one-sided that one party must
prevail as a matter of law. Id. at 251-52. Credibility determinations, the weighing of evidence, and
the drawing of legitimate inferences are jury functions, and the nonmovant's evidence is believed
with justifiable inferences drawn in its favor. Id. at 255.
Plaintiff bears the burden on the component he submits. He must show that the record
permits only one conclusion on it: that Hall was NCMEC's employee performing NCMEC's
business when she signed and issued the letters. The Court assesses the record with the inferences
the rule requires in Defendants' favor. Anderson states the general standard. It did not decide an
agency question, and Plaintiff does not cite it for one.
B.
The evidentiary foundations.
Rule 56(c)(1)(A) permits a fact to be supported by citing particular parts of the record,
including documents, declarations, and admissions. Rule 56(c)(4) requires a declaration to be made
9

on personal knowledge, to set out facts that would be admissible in evidence, and to show the
declarant's competence. Plaintiff's facts rest on four foundations, and each does a different job.
First, authentication. Plaintiff's declarations identify the earlier joint filing of NCMEC and
Hall, the letters, and the April 9 materials as true and correct copies obtained from identified
sources. ECF No. 7-1 19 4-6; Ballentine Decl. 19l 2-4. The copies of the letters in the record are
reproduced from the exhibits NCMEC and Hall themselves filed in the earlier action. ECF No. 7-
195; Ballentine Decl. 9 3. Authentication establishes what a document is. It does not establish the
truth of every assertion in the document.
Second, document contents. The letters and the April 9 materials are in the record. ECF
Nos. 7-5, 7-6. Their wording is a fact about them.
Third, opposing-party representations. The statements of NCMEC and Hall in ECF Nos.
11 and 45, and in the joint filing reproduced at ECF No. 7-4, are statements of the parties whose
relationship is at issue.
Fourth, personal-knowledge testimony. Plaintiff's declarations state what Plaintiff did.
ECF No. 31 11 1, 8; ECF No. 59-2 9 1.
C.
Virginia law supplies the substantive test and the effect of its presumption.
Counts I, II, III, and VI arise under Virginia law. Virginia law supplies the test for scope
of employment. Where state law supplies the rule of decision, state law governs the effect of a
presumption regarding the claim. Fed. R. Evid. 302. The Virginia presumption discussed in Part
V therefore carries the effect Virginia gives it.
. It does not displace the summary-judgment
standard, which remains federal.
10

V.
THE DOCUMENTS AND THE REPRESENTATIONS OF NCMEC AND HALL
SUPPORT THE AGENCY-AND-SCOPE DETERMINATION
A.
Virginia law asks whether the employee was performing the employer's
business within the scope of the employment.
"[A]n employer is liable for the tortious act of his employee if the employee was
performing his employer's business and acting within the scope of his employment." Parker v.
Carilion Clinic, 296 Va. 319, 335, 819 S.E.2d 809 (2018) (citation omitted). The inquiry asks
whether "the service itself, in which the tortious act was done, was within the ordinary course of
[the employer's] business." Id. at 336 (citation omitted). The act must have been "within the scope
of the duties of the employment and in the execution of the service for which the employee was
engaged." Id. at 338-39 (quotation marks and citation omitted). The employee must have
committed the act "while actively engaged in a job-related service." Id. at 339. Presence at work,
use of the employer's property, and the employer's time are not enough. Id.
Parker reviewed a demurrer. The court held that the allegations permitted the vicarious-
liability claim to proceed. It did not award the plaintiff judgment on the scope of employment.
Plaintiff cites Parker for the test it states and for the presumption it describes, not for its result.
B.
The service Hall performed was NCMEC's response to materials directed to
NCMEC's Legal Department.
The question is what service Hall was performing when she signed and issued the letters.
The record describes it. Plaintiff directed his April 9 materials to NCMEC's Legal Department.
Fact 4; ECF No. 7-6 at 2. NCMEC received them. Fact 4; ECF No. 7-4 at 3. NCMEC then
"responded." ECF No. 11 at 2. It responded "via two substantively-identical letters signed by
Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC." Id. The letters speak for
NCMEC: "the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children ("NCMEC") provides its written
responses as detailed below." Fact 3. They issued on NCMEC's letterhead, over the title

"Corporate Counsel." Fact 2. NCMEC calls them NCMEC's responses. ECF No. 11 at 3
(''NCMEC responded precisely as requested"); ECF No. 7-4 at 3 ("NCMEC responded exactly as
instructed in the subpoenas"). Hall adopts that description. ECF No. 45 at 1. And in the earlier
action, NCMEC and Hall described the same conduct as within Hall's employment. ECF No. 7-4
at 7.
Each of those items describes the same service: the issuance of NCMEC's legal
correspondence, by NCMEC's in-house counsel, concerning materials directed to NCMEC's
Legal Department. That service was NCMEC's business. The act at issue did not occur while Hall
happened to be at work. The act at issue was the work.
NCMEC's immunity argument states that "Plaintiff sent subpoenas to NCMEC seeking
information it received and maintains pursuant to its statutory charge, and NCMEC responded
precisely as requested," and that "the complained-of activity clearly relates to NCMEC's
clearinghouse role." ECF No. 11 at 8. NCMEC cannot argue that the letters were performance of
its statutory functions and also that Hall acted outside NCMEC's business.
C.
The employment presumption places the burden of production on NCMEC;
it does not relieve Plaintiff of his burden.
Once the employment relationship is established, Virginia law presumes that the employee
acted within the scope of employment. The presumption "shifts the burden of production to the
employer to present facts sufficient to permit the factfinder to conclude that the employee was not
acting within the scope of his employment at the time of his tortious conduct." Parker, 296 Va. at
333 n.6. The burden of persuasion remains with the plaintiff. Id. at 342. The presumption is
rebuttable; it gives way to positive facts to the contrary. Id. It operates at the stages at which the
sufficiency of the claim is tested, including summary judgment. Id. at 333 & n.6.
12

Plaintiff does not rest on the presumption. He rests on the letters and on the statements of
NCMEC and Hall about the service Hall performed. The presumption does one thing here. It
identifies NCMEC as the party that must come forward with facts of a departure from the
employment if NCMEC contends that one occurred. Whether the record then presents a genuine
dispute is decided under Rule 56 on the whole record.
D.
NCMEC and Hall have described the conduct as within the scope of Hall's
employment, and those statements are admissible against them.
Statements of a party's attorney concerning matters within the representation may be
admitted against the client. "Generally, statements by an attorney concerning a matter within his
employment may be admissible against the retaining client." United States v. Blood, 806 F.2d
1218, 1221 (4th Cir. 1986). Blood found no admission on its facts, and it did not resolve the
distinctions it noted between judicial and evidentiary admissions. Plaintiff relies on it for the
general proposition only. Federal Rule of Evidence 801(d)(2) treats as not hearsay a statement
offered against an opposing party that was made by a person the party authorized to make a
statement on the subject, or by the party's agent on a matter within the scope of that relationship
and while it existed. Fed. R. Evid. 801(d)(2)(C), (D). Counsel's statements in a signed filing on
behalf of a client, concerning the client's own employee and the client's own correspondence, fall
within those provisions. Rule 56(c)(1)(A) lists "admissions" among the materials that may support
a fact.
The earlier joint filing. Plaintiff's declaration authenticates the filing as the opposition
NCMEC and Hall filed at ECF No. 20 in the earlier action. ECF No. 7-1 9 4. The filing concerned
the same two letters and the same April 9 materials. ECF No. 7-4 at 2-3. It stated that Hall "is and
was an employee of the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, who was clearly
acting in the course and scope of her employment in responding to the subpoenas." Id. at 7. It
13

stated that Hall "was working within the course and scope of her employment, and is entitled to
the same defenses as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children." Id. Counsel signed
it for both Defendants. Id. at 9. Those statements were the stated ground for an argument the filing
made to the Court. Id. at 7. Plaintiff offers them against NCMEC and Hall, the parties who made
them, as evidentiary admissions. He does not contend that they are judicial admissions binding in
this action.
The current filings. NCMEC's memorandum states that the letters were "signed by
Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC," and that Hall "at all times
relevant was an employee of NCMEC." ECF No. 11 at 2, 5 n.2. Those sentences are NCMEC's
own descriptions of its employee and its correspondence. They are not recitations of Plaintiff's
allegations; the memorandum marks its recitations of the First Amended Complaint separately.
Compare id. at 2 ("Plaintiff alleges that on April 9, 2026 ..."), with id. (On April 22, 2026,
NCMEC responded ..."). Hall adopted the memorandum and described herself "as an employee
of NCMEC." ECF No. 45 at 1. The same counsel signed ECF No. 45 for both Defendants. Id. at
2. Plaintiff does not contend that every factual sentence in a dismissal brief is a binding judicial
admission. He contends that these particular sentences are statements of NCMEC and Hall about
their own relationship and their own conduct, and that Rule 56(c)(1)(A) and Rule 801(d)(2) permit
the Court to consider them.
Hall's footnote. Hall's description of herself carries a footnote citing Plaintiff's allegation
that she "served as Corporate Counsel of NCMEC." ECF No. 45 at 1 n.1. Hall asserted employee
status as the ground for her own relief: "because Ms. Hall, as an employee of NCMEC, enjoys
qualified statutory immunity under federal law." Id. at 1 (footnote omitted). A party that asks a
court to dismiss a claim because she is an employee has taken the position that she is one. The
14

footnote identifies a source. It does not withdraw the position. Hall also "adopts and joins in" ECF
No. 11. Id. That memorandum states independently of any allegation that the letters were "signed
by Defendant Hall, in her capacity as in-house counsel for NCMEC," ECF No. 11 at 2, and that
"she at all times relevant was an employee of NCMEC," id. at 5 n.2. It refers to "NCMEC or its
employee, Defendant Hall." Id. at 8.
Motive. The First Amended Complaint alleges that Hall acted with knowledge and with
actual malice. Alleged intentional wrongdoing does not itself place an employee outside the scope
of employment. Parker nevertheless treats the employee's motive as relevant to the scope inquiry.
296 Va. at 340-41. Plaintiff therefore relies on the evidence that describes the service Hall
performed: NCMEC's own responses, signed by its Corporate Counsel, concerning materials
directed to its Legal Department. The First Amended Complaint alleges that NCMEC approved
the letters and authorized the use of its name and letterhead. ECF No. 5 19 168, 196. Those
allegations identify Plaintiff's theory. They are not summary-judgment evidence, and Plaintiff
does not offer them as such.
E.
The determination reaches employment and scope, and nothing else.
The determination establishes that Hall was NCMEC's employee performing NCMEC's
business when she signed and issued the letters. It establishes nothing else. It does not establish
that any tort occurred. It does not establish that the letters were made in a judicial proceeding for
purposes of the litigation privilege NCMEC asserts, ECF No. 11 at 5, or that they were not. It does
not establish that the letters arose from CyberTipline responsibilities or functions under 18 U.S.C.
§ 2258D, or that they did not. Scope of employment under Virginia common law and statutory
function under § 2258D are different questions. The determination does not establish NCMEC's
direct liability for its own conduct, ECF No. 5 9 21, any requirement for punitive recovery, or any
15

defense. It does not reach any other person's conduct. Each of those matters remains for later
adjudication.
VI.
THE ACCOUNT-NAME AND DOCUMENT-HISTORY FACTS ARE
MATERIAL AND WARRANT SEPARATE CONSIDERATION UNDER RULE
56(g)
A.
Plaintiff's account-name history bears on the identification dispute framed
by the pleading and by NCMEC.
The First Amended Complaint alleges that the letters identify Plaintiff by two names and
an email address, ECF No. 5 9| 70; that the name "Jay Ballentine," standing alone, is not uniquely
identifying, id. 9 95; that the letters do not state whether any identifier appeared in any report, id.
9 96; and that a reader would understand the letters to associate Plaintiff personally with the
reports, id. 19 100-01. Counts I, II, and VI rest on that association. Id. 19 187-91, 208-12, 255.
NCMEC's memorandum addresses the same identifiers. It argues that Plaintiff cannot plead falsity
because "he does not have access to those reports," and it describes the possibility that "they, or a
person with the same name, or their e-mail address" is linked with a report. ECF No. 11 at 9. That
passage identifies three possible referents. It does not establish that the reports concern different
people, and it does not establish what NCMEC knows about the referents. It shows that the
connection between each identifier and Plaintiff personally is in dispute.
Facts 8 through 12 bear on that dispute. They separate the name Plaintiff used to litigate
from the names Plaintiff used on Meta's services. Plaintiff did not use his legal name to operate
any Meta account he used. Facts 8-10. He operated the Facebook account involved in the July 4,
2022 enforcement action under the name "Jay Ballentine." Fact 11. His legal name appears in the

VII. THE COURT MAY TREAT PROPERLY SUPPORTED FACTS AS
UNDISPUTED WITHIN THE LIMITS OF RULE 56(e)
A.
The sequence under Rule 56(c) and Rule 56(e).
Rule 56(c)(1) requires a party asserting that a fact cannot be or is genuinely disputed to
support the assertion by citing particular parts of the record, or by showing that the materials cited
do not establish the absence or presence of a genuine dispute, or that an adverse party cannot
produce admissible evidence to support the fact. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(1)(A)-(B). Rule 56(c)(2)
permits an objection that cited material cannot be presented in a form that would be admissible in
evidence. Local Civil Rule 56(B) requires an opposing brief to include a specifically captioned
section listing the material facts the opponent contends are genuinely in issue, with citations to the
parts of the record relied on. The local rule then provides: "In determining a motion for summary
judgment, the Court may assume that facts identified by the moving party in its listing of material
facts are admitted, unless such a fact is controverted in the statement of genuine issues filed in
opposition to the motion."
18

The sequence is this. First, Plaintiff must support each asserted fact. Part III does so.
Second, an opposing party may challenge the evidence: its sufficiency to establish the proposition,
its admissibility, or its materiality. A legal argument that the cited materials do not establish the
proposition is a proper response under Rule 56(c)(1)(B). An objection under Rule 56(c)(2) is a
proper response. A showing of immateriality is a proper response. Third, a bare contradiction
without record support is not sufficient. Fourth, where a fact is properly supported and not properly
addressed, the Court may give an opportunity to address it, consider it undisputed for purposes of
the Motion, or issue another appropriate order. Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(e)(1), (2), (4). Fifth, any
establishment of a fact in the action, beyond this Motion, requires separate consideration under
Rule 56(g).
B.
Motion-specific treatment and case-wide treatment are different.
Rule 56(e)(2) permits the Court to consider a fact undisputed "for purposes of the motion."
Local Civil Rule 56(B) permits the same assumption in determining the Motion. Neither
establishes a fact for trial. Rule 56(g) reaches further. When the Court does not grant all the relief
requested by the motion, it "may enter an order stating any material fact... that is not genuinely
in dispute and treating the fact as established in the case." Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(g). Plaintiff requests
the two forms of treatment in that order and keeps them distinct.
A Defendant may accept a fact for purposes of this Motion only. Rule 56(c)(1)(A)
recognizes stipulations "made for purposes of the motion only." Plaintiff's express request under
Rule 56(g) gives notice that each numbered fact is offered for establishment in the action. That
notice does not convert a limited acceptance into an unlimited one. A Defendant that accepts a fact
for the Motion only may say so in its statement of genuine issues, and the Court may take that
limitation into account in deciding whether to establish the fact under Rule 56(g). Plaintiff does

not contend that any Defendant's earlier briefing operates as a response to this Motion. The
oppositions to this Motion are where each fact is to be addressed.
VIll. ANY CLAIMED NEED FOR DISCOVERY SHOULD BE EVALUATED
AGAINST THE PARTICULAR DETERMINATION IT AFFECTS
As a general rule, summary judgment is appropriate only after adequate time for discovery.
Harrods Ltd. v. Sixty Internet Domain Names, 302 F.3d 214, 244 (4th Cir. 2002). Rule 56(d)
supplies the mechanism. A nonmovant that cannot present facts essential to its opposition may
show that by affidavit or declaration, "for specified reasons," and the Court may defer considering
the motion, deny it, allow time for discovery, or issue any other appropriate order. Fed. R. Civ. P.
56(d). The Fourth Circuit gives such a showing great weight. Harrods, 302 F.3d at 244. The court
has also recognized that a nonmovant's objections may serve as the functional equivalent of an
affidavit where they adequately inform the district court of the discovery needed and the
nonmovant has not been lax in pursuing it. Id. at 244-45; see Pledger v. Lynch, 5 F.4th 511, 526
(4th Cir. 2021) (applying that principle to the objections of a pro se prisoner). Harrods applied the
predecessor of current Rule 56(d). Plaintiff does not ask the Court to hold any Defendant to a form.
He asks that any claimed need be stated for the fact it affects.
Harrods identified circumstances in which early summary judgment carries particular risk:
where the relevant facts are exclusively in the control of the opposing party, and where the case
involves complex factual questions about intent and motive. 302 F.3d at 246 47. The agency-and-
scope component should be evaluated against those circumstances. The facts concern Hall's
employment, the capacity in which she acted, and the service she performed when she signed
NCMEC's correspondence. NCMEC and Hall have described those matters themselves, in this
action and in the earlier one. The Motion asks the Court to consider those descriptions and the
letters. If NCMEC or Hall contends that discovery is needed before the Court can assess the
